They are softer than wood sticks and give you a very smooth effect when opening vessels.

tools.name: 7.5" Steel Standard Jacks
tools.description: These jacks dont mess around. Nice stout blades that carry their mass further down the blade compared to the cup jacks. Great all around tool for all occasions. If you are a student looking for your first pair of jacks, this is what you want.

tools.name: 8” bronze standard jacks
tools.description: These have Beefier blades and are a stouter version of the cup jacks which have finer tips. Why bronze? Theres a bunch of reasons why I chose to make jacks with bronze blades. Firstly, bronze is softer than steel and gives you a very smooth experience when working hot glass with them. Bronze does not chill glass like steel does. The result of this is that you gain working time, which means you might be able to make a piece in less reheats. Because the bronze blades do not cool the glass like steel does, your jack lines will be less prone to creating chill marks, which is the number one cause of wear on jack blades. With this logic one can assume that a pair of bronze jacks could outlast a pair of steel jacks if used with care. Also, bronze does not rust ! Bronze is not for everything and should not replace steel for times when force is needed, or used for prolonged use on very thick hot glass.

tools.name: 9" Steel Oval Jacks
tools.description: Based of of Dino Tedeshi’s oval jack design, these jacks are very unique. The fat oval blades are perfect for squeezing down on a jack line when you want to keep things a little thicker up there. Its counter intuitive but I have found that I can get thinner lips when i use these because you have more mass to tweeze and trim. Also if you watch some videos of pino working his magic you might notice he uses this style jack. They are also wonderful for flaring because the rounded edges of the blades just allow a small amount of steel to ride on the surface of the glass which equates to less drag.

tools.name: 9” standard Bronze jacks
tools.description: A more robust beefier blade suitable for 2 or 3 gather pieces.

tools.name: 9” Steel Standard Jacks

tools.description: D2 Trim shears made with great care one at a time. The geometry of the shears was influenced by my favorite pair of Jim Moore trim shears that I have been using for the past 30 years. They are razor sharp and cut very well.

tools.description: These fun little jacks are loosely based off of Ivan Smith’s Small Liquer Jacks that he nicknamed “pig stickers”. They are my favorite pair of jacks that he made and use them for smaller work. They would be good for a lampworker or anyone who finds a longer blade cumbersome for fine detailed work.

tools.name: Medium tweezers
tools.description: Simple Murano style pincetta tweezers. Beaked to really grab and hang on when tweezing lips, pulling out bubbles or crud in hot gathers and also hold water nicely. Not to light. Not too heavy. The goldielocks tweezer.

tools.name: Pacioffi handles (parchoffi)
tools.description: Classic Ennion jack handles with stainless steel tubing brazed in to hold wood or cardboard tubes. Keep them waxed up and they will last a long time.

tools.name: Screw on Pacioffi (parchoffi) handles
tools.description: This style handle used to be quite popular in the 80’s and 90’s, but then the source for the cardboard tubes dried up. I now have a source for the tubes so heres the handles ! You treat the tubes like you would treat a newspaper shaping pad. Give them an initial soak for 5 minutes and then quick dips between pieces or spritz water on them. When burned in they leave zero tool marks and are great for making bowls or any wide opening that you want to look flawless. On smaller pieces i will quickly give openings a little flare with regular jacks to make the opening wide enough to fit the tubes in and then go for the carboard pacioffis.

tools.name: Steel Cup Jacks
tools.description: I designed these cupjacks as a cross between Ivan Smith’s small Liquer jacks (he called them pig stickers) and Jim Moore’s cup jacks. The blades on these are approximately 7.5” long. Obviously they are great for cups but the fun doesn't end there. Pumpkins, ornaments, anything in the 1 to 2 gather range is fair game.

tools.name: Steel Goblet Jacks
tools.description: With thinner blades than the cupjacks and pointier tips, these jacks mean business. I shape the blades to give them the shape of an almond so that the blades don't want to drag on the inside of the vessel wall. It's just a little detail I have picked up along the way of making jacks. If you were to ask me what my dream pair of goblet jacks would be like, this is it!
